title: Model: multi-period selection with all section 6 rules

blocks.text: 13.1.2 Model: Multi-Period Selection With All Section 6 Rules

The snapshot of lesson 13.1.1 is accepted, and the planners ask the question CIPT exists for: which of GridCap medium's 400 projects should start, and in which of the ten years, to get the most NPV while every business rule holds? Section 6 wrote each rule on its own, often on a model that had only that rule. The milestone puts every rule GridCap's data carries into one model, gives every row the name the planners will read in a diagnosis, and then asks how anyone can trust what the model returns: the solve stops at a stated gap, the plan is checked by code that never sees the model, and hand-built plans test each rule from both sides. GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio.
The Model

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan years (2027 to 2036); $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years of project $`i`$, those in its window whose every year of work falls inside $`Y`$ (lesson 6.4.1); $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups, each a set $`g \subseteq P`$ (lesson 6.5.3); $`C \subseteq P`$ the children, each with its parent $`p(c)`$; $`R`$ the regions and $`P_r`$ the projects in region $`r`$; $`K`$ the programs (transmission, distribution, vegetation) and $`P_k`$ the projects in program $`k`$; from the scenario, $`F`$ the projects forced in, $`O`$ the projects forced out, and $`S`$ the projects whose start year $`t_i`$ is fixed (lesson 6.5.6).

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ the NPV of project $`i`$ if it starts in $`t`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$ what it spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k), with $`d_i`$ years of work and $`\text{capex}_i = \sum_k c_{i,k}`$; $`L_c`$ the lag between parent and child (years); $`B_y`$ the year's budget and $`B_{r,y}`$ the region's ($k); $`m_i`$ the crew-months project $`i`$ uses in each year of work and $`W_{k,y}`$ the crew-months program $`k`$ has in year $`y`$; $`\Phi_r`$ the least region $`r`$ must receive over the plan ($k), a rate-case commitment (lesson 6.5.5).

**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$. Write $`s_i = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$ (1 if the project is funded) and $`\text{spend}_{i,y} = \sum_{t \in T_i,\; 0 \le y - t < d_i} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t}`$ (lesson 6.4.2). Overrides are bounds: $`x_{i,t} = 1`$ if $`t = t_i`$ and $`0`$ otherwise for $`i \in S`$, and $`x_{i,t} = 0`$ for $`i \in O`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
s_i &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
s_i &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
s_i &\ge 1 && \forall i \in F && \text{(force}_i) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} s_i &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\textstyle\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \textstyle\sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P} \text{spend}_{i,y} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P_r} \text{spend}_{i,y} &\le B_{r,y} && \forall r \in R,\ y \in Y && \text{(region}_{r,y}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P_k} \sum_{t \in T_i,\; t \le y < t + d_i} m_i\, x_{i,t} &\le W_{k,y} && \forall k \in K,\ y \in Y && \text{(crews}_{k,y}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P_r} \text{capex}_i\, s_i &\ge \Phi_r && \forall r \in R && \text{(floor}_r)
\end{aligned}

The precedence row is the cumulative form of lesson 6.4.3: by every year $`t`$, the child may have started only if its parent started at least $`L_c`$ years earlier. Each row's code name is its label with the indices filled in: `must_P097`, `after_P012_2035`, `region_Coast_2031`, `crews_transmission_2029`.
Every Rule GridCap's Data Carries Is a Named Row

The model has exactly the rules the snapshot has data for. Section 6 taught more forms (carry-over budgets in 6.4.4, piecewise costs in 6.6.1 to 6.6.3, symmetry rows in 6.7.3), and each needs data GridCap's export does not carry: a carry-over rate, a cost curve, identical assets. A rule without its data would be a row with invented numbers, so CIPT Lite leaves them out and says so.
`build` writes each row with its name and keeps a map from name to row, so that milestone 4 can switch rows off by name and milestone 6 can report them. The precedence rows, for instance:

for c in portfolio.projects:                                          # (after_{c,t}), cumulative form
        if c.parent:
            parent = by_id[c.parent]
            for t in c.starts():
                b.add(f"after_{c.project_id}_{t}",
                      mathopt.LinearExpression()
                      + mathopt.fast_sum(x[c.project_id, u] for u in c.starts() if u <= t)
                      - mathopt.fast_sum(x[parent.project_id, s] for s in parent.starts()
                                         if s <= t - c.parent_lag) <= 0)

The sum starts from an empty `mathopt.LinearExpression()`, because a parent with no start early enough gives an empty sum, which is the number 0, and a comparison of plain numbers is a Python `bool` that MathOpt refuses as a row. The three money and crew families share one pass over the start variables, so each project's spread cost is computed once and every rule about money uses the same expression (lesson 6.4.2):
`model_medium.py` counts what GridCap medium becomes:
887 start variables, 543 rows: after 41, alt 18, budget 10, crews 30, floor 4, must 39, once 361, region 40

39 must and 361 once rows make one per project; 41 precedence rows come from 18 children, one per start year each child has; 30 crew rows are three programs over ten years, and 40 regional rows are four regions over ten years.
A Run Stops at a Stated Gap, and Its Plan Is Checked Without the Model
How long to let HiGHS search is a decision, and CIPT Lite states it once, as its **run setting**: a relative gap of 0.1% and one thread.

`HIGHS` sets `threads` to 1 in HiGHS's own options, because HiGHS through MathOpt refuses the common `threads` parameter and fixes its count at the first solve of a process (lesson 10.2.2). One thread is what lets milestone 5 promise the same plan on every run. The gap is the stopping rule of lesson 3.4.2: stop once the plan is proved within 0.1% of the best possible. Here is the run, and the same model solved to a zero gap for comparison:

run setting (gap 0.1%): OPTIMAL, NPV 219,054, bound 219,273, gap 0.1000%, 791 nodes, 209 projects
NPV recomputed from the data: 219,054; rules broken: []
zero gap (reference):   OPTIMAL, NPV 219,208, 26,516 nodes
run within 0.1% of the reference: True (0.0703% below it)

`OPTIMAL` under a gap means "proved within the gap", not "the best plan" (lesson 3.4.3). The run setting's plan is $154k below the plan the zero-gap solve finds, and the zero-gap solve searched 26,516 nodes against 791 to prove that last 0.07%. On a $219,000k portfolio whose inputs are forecasts, CIPT Lite takes the 0.1% and reports the bound beside the plan. So "the objective equals the reference within tolerance" has a precise meaning in this milestone: the run's NPV is at least the reference times $`(1 - 0.001)`$.
The second line is the other half of trust. `check` reads only the snapshot, the scenario and the plan, and recomputes every rule from the data:

def check(portfolio: Portfolio, scenario: Scenario, plan: dict[str, int]) -> list[str]:
    """Every rule the plan breaks, by row name, computed from the data alone (no model, no solver)."""

It returns the names of the rows the plan breaks, in the model's own names. A wrong row in `build` cannot approve its own plan, because `check` never looks at the rows (lesson 12.3.2). Every milestone from here on runs `check` on every plan it reports, and the service of milestone 6 refuses to return a plan that fails it.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Hand-Built Plans Test Each Rule From Both Sides

A solve tests the model at one point: the plan it returned. Lesson 12.3.1 showed that a rule can be wrong and still leave that plan unchanged, so the model needs testing on plans chosen by hand. `allows` fixes every start variable by its bounds (1 for each start in the plan, 0 for every other) and asks HiGHS whether the fixed model is feasible. A start the model has no variable for is refused before any solve. `model_medium.py` starts from the solver's plan and changes it so that one rule breaks (the fewest rows it can, searched from the data), then asks both the model and the checker:

the solver's plan                            model: allowed  checker: no rule broken
P024 (must-do) left out                      model: refused  checker: must_P024
P012 kept, its parent P011 left out          model: refused  checker: after_P012_2035
P003 added beside its alternative            model: refused  checker: alt_G002, crews_distribution_2027
P004 ($590k) added in 2035                   model: refused  checker: budget_2035
P004 (1 crew-months) added in 2036           model: refused  checker: crews_distribution_2036

Read the table from both sides. The first row is the **allowed** side: a valid plan must pass, or a rule is too strict, which no check of the solver's own plans can reveal. The other rows are the **refused** side, each naming the rule it targets. A row made stricter still refuses every plan built to break it, so the refused side cannot catch a rule that is too strict. P003's row breaks two rules: of all the additions of one alternative in one start year that the program tried, none broke the alternative row alone, and this one, which also needs a distribution crew-month the plan has already used in 2027, was the best it found. The test is still sound: the model refuses, and the checker names the rule the row was built to break.

The model and the checker agree on all six. They are two implementations of the same rules, written from the formulation independently, so their agreement on plans built to break each rule is the evidence that both are right. When they disagree, one of them has a bug, and the plan in that row is the smallest case to debug.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Every rule GridCap's data carries is a named row.** Once, must, force, alternatives, cumulative precedence, yearly, regional and crew limits, and regional floors: 887 variables and 543 rows on GridCap medium, each row named by its label.

**A run stops at a stated gap, and its plan is checked without the model.** One thread and a 0.1% gap: $219,054k proved within 0.1%, $154k below the zero-gap plan. `check` recomputes every rule from the data and found nothing broken.
**Hand-built plans test each rule from both sides.** The solver's plan must be allowed; plans built to break one rule must be refused; the model and the checker agree on all of them.

Challenges

items: Add the carry-over budget of lesson 6.4.4 with a rate of 50%. Which data must the snapshot gain, which rows change, and which hand-built plan would show the new rule from its allowed side?
P003's hand-built plan broke two rules. Build a plan by hand that breaks `alt_G002` alone. What did you have to drop to make room?
The run's plan and the reference plan both pass `check`. Which of them should the service report, and what must it print beside it?

blocks.text: Design Note: Two Implementations of One Formulation

`build` and `check` are written from the same formulation and share no code. That duplication is deliberate. A test that solves the model and checks the plan with the model's own rows can only confirm the model agrees with itself. A checker that recomputes spend, crews and precedence from the data is a second reading of the formulation, and the hand-built plans are where the two readings meet. The cost is keeping both in step when a rule changes; the formulation block is the contract both follow.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**model_medium.py.** Builds GridCap medium, counts its rows, solves it with the run setting and to a zero gap, and puts hand-built plans to the model and the checker (every section). *Try:* Change the run's gap to 0.5%. Predict whether the plan still breaks no rule, and how far from the reference its NPV lands.
The milestone's library is `cipt_model.py`.
